Part 1

What must the controls of this unit achieve, and how many independent loops can it have?

Part 1 · the plan

From objectives to a count of handles

  1. Control objectivessix, in a fixed order of priority
  2. The feedback loopmeasurement, controller, final element, process
  3. Degrees of freedom20 = 8 disturbances + 12 handles
  4. The loops on the P&IDfifteen controllers, twelve handles

Interactive — pick a priority

Six objectives, in a fixed order

People and equipment first, then product, then rate and cost.

When two objectives conflict, the higher one wins — the anti-surge loops stay in AUTO whatever the operator does with speed.

Counting before pairing

How many variables can be held?

Each independent handle can hold one variable, no more.

$N_{var}$
variables of the steady state
–
$N_{eq}$
independent equations: balances, equilibria, valve and compressor equations
–
$N_{DV}$
disturbances, set by the surroundings
–
$N_{MV}$
handles: valves and driver speeds
–
$$N_{DOF}=N_{var}-N_{eq}=N_{DV}+N_{MV}$$
$40-20=20=8+12$this unit: twenty dependent variables, one equation each

Too many controllers fight; too few leave variables drifting.

Interactive — click a bubble

Fifteen controllers on one drawing

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • Six objectives, safety first, energy last; the higher one wins.
  • Every loop: sensor, controller, final element, process; action and fail position.
  • $N_{DOF}$ = 20 = 8 disturbances + 12 handles.
  • Fifteen controllers − three cascade masters = twelve handles in use.

Part 2 · the plan

Pairing and structure

  1. Rules for choosing loopsdirect, fast, one sign; fast loops inside

Rules used on this P&ID

Four rules decide the pairing

Twelve handles are counted; now each gets its variable.

Objectives and DOF first

Twelve handles, twelve jobs; none for a balance.

Direct, fast, one sign

Step tests give gain, lag and dead time.

Fast loops inside

Levels and flows inside; temperatures on top.

Protection apart

Anti-surge always in AUTO; trips outside the loops.

Interactive — pick a candidate pair

Nine pairings tested, four chosen

The rejected handles work too — they lose on side effects: throttling losses, a shared header, a slow analyser.

Why the levels are the handles

Wetted area sets the kettle duty

$Q$
kettle duty
kW
$U$
overall heat-transfer coefficient
kW/(m²·K)
$A_w$
tube area wetted by boiling refrigerant, grows with level $L$
m²
$\Delta T_{lm}$
log-mean gas − refrigerant temperature difference
K
$$Q=U\,A_w(L)\,\Delta T_{lm}$$

Boiling temperature is fixed by suction pressure: PI-201 1.355 bar a holds −40 °C.

Single loop or cascade

The level loop corrects first

A level is fast, a gas temperature slow: nest them.

Same handle LV-108, one DOF; the inner loop is 3–5× faster.

Interactive — pick a structure

Nine structures, five used here

Feedback, cascade, anti-surge and trips cover this unit — no stream must follow another, so ratio and split range have no job.

UI-205 surge marginFV-205 opening

Less feed, less flow through K-201: only the recycle adds flow without adding load, and only PI returns the margin to set point.

Kettle fills, receiver empties

The receivers had no handle; here is why none is needed.

LI-108 kettleLI-312 receiverLIC-108 set point

The ethylene charge stays 6.7 t — what LI-108 gains, LI-312 loses; a loop on LI-312 would fight TIC-107.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • Pair each CV with a direct, fast, one-sign handle.
  • Kettles: level sets wetted area, so level sets duty.
  • Cascades: TIC-102, TIC-107, PIC-310 act through their level loops.
  • Anti-surge recycles protect the machines; receiver levels follow the charge.

Part 3

How is each loop modelled from a step test, and how fast should it be tuned?

Part 3 · the plan

Model, tune, check on the plant

  1. The PI controllerwhat P, I and D each do
  2. Step test and FOPDT fitgain, time constant, dead time of eight loops
  3. Lambda tuningtwo presets: robust and tight
  4. Check on the modelFOPDT prediction against the simulator run

The simulator’s controller

Ideal PID, error in % of span

Pairing chose the handle; tuning sets how hard it moves.

$OUT$
controller output, valve opening
%
$e$
error: SP% − PV% (reverse) or PV% − SP% (direct)
%
$K_c$
controller gain
%/%
$T_i,\ T_d$
integral time, derivative time
s
$$OUT=K_c\,e+\frac{K_c}{T_i}\int e\,dt-K_c\,T_d\,\frac{dPV\%}{dt}$$

P only leaves an offset; I removes it; D unused here.

Identifying the process

A 5 % step in MAN gives three numbers

$K$
process gain, PV change per OUT change
%/%
$\tau$
time constant
s
$\theta$
dead time
s
$t_{28},\ t_{63}$
times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change
s
$$\Delta PV\%(t)=K\,\Delta OUT\left(1-e^{-(t-\theta)/\tau}\right),\ t>\theta$$
$K=\dfrac{\Delta PV\%}{\Delta OUT\%}\quad \tau=1.5\,(t_{63}-t_{28})\quad \theta=t_{63}-\tau$two-point fit used by the tab

Interactive — fit the model run by hand

Eight step tests on the simulator

model runFOPDT

The cascade masters fit $\theta > \tau$: a slave level and an exchanger seen through it look like dead time.

Lambda (IMC) PI tuning

Ask for a closed-loop time constant $\lambda$

From the step test$K,\ \tau,\ \theta$ of the FOPDT fit
$\lambda$
closed-loop time constant asked for
s
$$K_c=\frac{\tau}{|K|\,(\lambda+\theta)}\qquad T_i=\tau$$
$\lambda=\max(\tau,\,3\theta)$“lambda” preset: robust when dead time is large
$\lambda=\max(\tau/3,\,\theta)$“tight” preset: never faster than the dead time
TIC-107: $\lambda=\max(77,377)=377$ s, $K_c=\dfrac{77}{0.247\times 503}=0.62$$T_i$ = 77 s

Levels: $K_c=(2\lambda+\theta)/(K_i(\lambda+\theta)^2)$, $T_i=2\lambda+\theta$; $\lambda$ 300 s or 100 s.

Interactive — FOPDT + PI, set-point step

Faster tuning, larger overshoot

Push $\lambda$ below $\theta$ and the overshoot climbs — dead time, not the time constant, limits how tight a loop can be.

Interactive — the same tunings on the simulator

The model has the last word

The FOPDT is a fit; the simulator is the plant.

For TIC-107 tight, the FOPDT predicts 4 % overshoot; the simulator gives 76 % — a fit with $\theta > \tau$ hides a slower process.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • PI on almost every loop; integral removes the offset P leaves.
  • A 5 % step in MAN gives $K$, $\tau$, $\theta$ by the two-point fit.
  • Lambda tuning: $K_c=\tau/(|K|(\lambda+\theta))$, $T_i=\tau$.
  • Large dead time calls for slow tuning; check every tuning on the model.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Rank the objectives and count the degrees of freedom before drawing any loop.

2

Give each handle one variable; leave the receiver levels to the charge.

3

Control kettles by level, and put slow temperatures on top as cascade masters.

4

Fit a step test, tune with $\lambda \ge \theta$, then check the tuning on the model.
